prompt.context: Our client is a large industrial conglomerate with $60-70 million in annual revenues that is extremely profitable. They have engaged BCG to examine one of their business units that is underperforming. The unit manufactures and distributes street sweepers (zamboni/lawnmower-like machines that a person rides and which uses two large rotating brushes to sweep up the street as it moves by) and has been doing so for 20 years. While never a standout division, until recently it had always been profitable. 4-5 years ago the profit margins started to fall and it is currently just above breakeven. Management of the conglomerate made a decision 2 years ago that they did not want to invest in new features for their product lines and has the approach that they don't want to invest significant amounts of capital now (unless they can be convinced otherwise).
prompt.question: BCG's task is to analyze the unit's performance and recommend to the management of the conglomerate what should be done. Tell me some of the areas you'd consider looking into here, knowing that we only have a few weeks to finish this engagement.

clarifying_info.q: What has happened to costs over time?
clarifying_info.a: Costs have been fairly constant over the past 20 years, only increasing with inflation.
Revenue has fallen steadily over the past 5 years.

Mostly state and local governments (municipalities). They are keeping with past trends, replacing their street sweepers every 4-7 years, and the number of municipalities purchasing street sweepers has remained constant.

clarifying_info.q: Have new competitors entered the market?
clarifying_info.a: There have been no new competitors.

clarifying_info.q: What is competitor B doing differently?
clarifying_info.a: About 5 years ago, B introduced a new technology using air vacuums to clean streets instead of mechanical collecting methods. Air machines are more effective at picking up small debris like sand and small litter, and work more quickly and efficiently. Price points are about the same. B still sells mechanical machines, but the drop in our client's market share was directly related to the new air offering.

clarifying_info.q: What is competitor C doing differently?
clarifying_info.a: C makes machines that are far more heavy-duty; it is really a different type of offering in a niche market.

clarifying_info.q: Can our client replicate the air technology?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, but it will take 2 years and cost $25 million.

clarifying_info.q: Do municipalities need both mechanical and air sweepers?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, they need both. The country is divided into 7 regions, all needing the same total number of street sweepers. In the north, the average ratio of mechanical to air sweepers is 22:8. In the south, it is 22:18 (these numbers do not include C's models).

exhibits.title: Market Share Over Time
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart showing the market share split among three competitors (Client A, B, and C) at three points in time: 10 years ago, 5 years ago, and today.
exhibits.data: Three time periods shown: 10 years ago, 5 years ago, today. Three competitors: C (top), B (middle), Client A (bottom). Client A's share has declined significantly from 10 years ago to today, while B's share has grown correspondingly. C's share appears roughly stable.

framework: Investigate costs: have they changed over time (inflation, input costs, fixed vs variable)?
Investigate revenues: volume (units sold) vs price vs mix
Explore revenue drivers: customer behavior, market size, pricing, competition
Analyze competitive dynamics: who took share, how, and why
Assess strategic options given capital constraint: defend current position, enter new segment, divest

questions.prompt: What has driven the profit decline?
questions.guidance: Costs have been stable (only inflation). Revenue has fallen steadily for 5 years. Therefore the decline is entirely revenue-driven. Candidate should narrow quickly to revenue analysis.

questions.prompt: What is driving the revenue decline — price, volume, or mix?
questions.guidance: Prices are constant. Customer count and replacement cycles are unchanged. Competition: no new entrants. Therefore volume (units sold / market share) must have fallen. Point to Exhibit 1 to show share loss to competitor B.

questions.prompt: After seeing Exhibit 1, what do you want to know and what does it tell you?
questions.guidance: Client (A) has lost significant share to B. C has remained stable. Candidate should identify: (1) what B did differently to gain share, and (2) why C is unaffected. Strong answer flags that C may be in a different sub-segment, not a true competitor.

questions.prompt: Should the client try to enter competitor C's heavy-duty segment?
questions.guidance: C has a stable niche, proprietary expertise, and no obvious vulnerability. Without a differentiated offering, entering C's segment would provoke defense of that niche. Likely not worth pursuing given capital constraints.

questions.prompt: Given air technology costs $25M and 2 years to replicate, and management does not want to invest significantly, what are realistic options?
questions.guidance: Replicating air technology is likely off the table given the capital constraint and timeline. Candidate should pivot to asking about the remaining market for mechanical sweepers — is there still a durable demand base?

questions.prompt: The country has 7 equal-sized regions. In the north the mechanical-to-air ratio is 22:8; in the south it is 22:18. Assume 4 northern regions and 3 southern regions. What percentage of total street sweeper sales will be mechanical?
questions.guidance: Calculate total mechanical and total air units across all 7 regions, then find the mechanical share. The answer is approximately 64-66%. This confirms a durable, substantial market for mechanical sweepers.

math.setup: 4 northern regions each need 22 mechanical + 8 air = 30 units. 3 southern regions each need 22 mechanical + 18 air = 40 units.
steps: North total: 4 x 30 = 120 units; mechanical in north: 4 x 22 = 88
South total: 3 x 40 = 120 units; mechanical in south: 3 x 22 = 66
math.answer: Approximately 64% of street sweeper sales will be mechanical (casebook cites ~66% as a reasonable estimate).

questions.prompt: Why do municipalities still need mechanical sweepers if air is more efficient?
questions.guidance: Mechanical sweepers handle larger, heavier debris (rocks, chunks of ice, etc.) that air cannot. Northern climates generate this debris more frequently. This is a structural demand, not a transitional one — mechanical sweepers serve a distinct functional need.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic options should BCG recommend to the conglomerate for the street sweeper unit?

categories.name: Defend & optimize mechanical position
ideas: Right-size production to match the ~64% mechanical share of a stable market
Cut costs to restore margins without capital investment
Focus sales efforts on northern regions with higher mechanical demand
Lock in long-term municipal contracts to protect remaining share

categories.name: Exit / divest
ideas: Sell the unit to a strategic buyer (e.g., a foreign firm with air technology)
Divest to a competitor who can integrate the mechanical business with air offerings
Wind down the unit in a controlled manner if no buyer is found

categories.name: Invest in air technology (conditional)
ideas: Only if management can be convinced to commit $25M over 2 years
Partner or license air technology rather than develop in-house to reduce cost and time

categories.name: Do nothing / harvest
ideas: Maintain current operations at near-breakeven while milking any residual cash
Accept gradual decline if no investment is made

recommendation: Recommend the conglomerate right-size the street sweeper unit to the defensible ~64% mechanical share of the market, reducing production to equilibrium between air and mechanical demand, which will restore margins without new capital investment.

Simultaneously, seek a strategic buyer — ideally a foreign firm that already has air technology — who could combine the client's mechanical distribution network with air offerings and create more value than the conglomerate can alone.
risks: Mechanical share could erode further if air technology improves and becomes applicable to heavy debris
Foreign or strategic buyer may not materialize, leaving the unit in a prolonged near-breakeven state
Right-sizing production requires managing workforce reductions and fixed-cost footprint
next_steps: Model the production and cost structure at equilibrium mechanical volume to confirm margin recovery
Identify and approach potential strategic buyers with existing air technology
Define a trigger point: if mechanical share falls below X% within N years, accelerate divestiture
